request:
A world in the PROTO-SOLARIS sector, kept after Stanisław Lem — Solaris.

The operations this world is built from:
- Living Planet: a universe where the biosphere or planet functions as an agent (life and evolution, scarcity shift).
- Impossible Contact: a universe where the parties do not share sufficient categories (contact and civilizations, substitution).

When we arrive: A planetary ocean responds to stimuli and appears to preserve geological patterns, but its consciousness cannot be tested without intrusion.

The central tension we want to continue: Aster admits that an earlier version of herself once tried to force such a world to “speak” and caused centuries of turbulence

What the course asks of this world: Stanisław Lem — Solaris.

sourceText: Aster did not announce the night’s theme. She opened the PROTO-SOLARIS sector and let the children discover for themselves which of the world’s rules concerned them directly. A planetary ocean responds to stimuli and appears to preserve geological patterns, but its consciousness cannot be tested without intrusion. The memorial bore the name of Stanisław Lem — Solaris precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin. During this period, the children were not allowed to call a species “superior” before stating exactly relative to what environment, what task, and what criterion. Tern had specialized in things that did not answer. In a family built for exploration, he had become the custodian of the right to silence. The children were met by Sera, who refused demonstrations. ‘If you can perform miracles, perform them after you tell me what becomes irreversible.’ Marae appreciated the formulation; Aster admitted that in earlier eras she herself would have asked the question only after optimizing. 161 The problem closed quickly around them: Aster admits that an earlier version of herself once tried to force such a world to “speak” and caused centuries of turbulence. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave. Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Lp — Living Planet: the biosphere or planet functions as an agent; Nc — Impossible Contact: the parties do not share sufficient categories. Course references included Stanisław Lem — Solaris. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder. Orin broke the first consensus. ‘I do not want the perfect branch. I want us to know what we sacrificed in order to call it perfect.’ Tern answered without raising their voice: ‘Sometimes the ethical question is whether we are entitled to know enough to optimize.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs. For Aster, the pain came not from too few worlds but from the fact that too many had become transparent. She could build variations faster than a human could formulate desires, but calculated variation did not produce exteriority. It was like trying to surprise yourself by moving objects around your own room with your eyes closed. 162 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS Vela evaluated the solution not by efficiency but by the differences it made invisible. She found one: a local minority for whom the proposed “improvement” destroyed a practice with no equivalent. Optimizing the average concealed a small and perfectly legal extinction. The night did not end in victory. Tern receives from the ocean the same signal of impossible provenance. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility. Tern no longer called the anomaly a “signal.” He used the more modest term residue. He found it only after excluding the explanations he wanted to be true. Vela helped precisely through skepticism: if a hypothesis survived a sister motivated to destroy it, it deserved another night. For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the OUTFINITE operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — allows successive finite extensions without postulating an already-given final infinite state — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of a mind, a copy of a world, and a copy of a history were not the same phenomenon, but they shared a conceptual chemistry. Vela introduced the propagation test: if you remove the speculative idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the 163 opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure. In the hall between sectors, Aster’s Hunger returned. None of the children tried to soothe it. They had begun to believe that some pains should not immediately be turned into demands upon the people nearby. 164 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS 165 PART 6​ HOW MANY PEOPLE FIT INSIDE A PERSON? A period in the curriculum of the five children 166 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS
